options.a: Objective reasonableness: force proportional to threat and applied only when necessary
options.b: The officer's subjective fear at the moment, even if a reasonable officer would not share it
options.c: A fixed force continuum that must be climbed one level at a time before any higher force
options.d: The outcome of the encounter, judged with hindsight after all facts are known to reviewers

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the objective test with a subjective one; courts ask what a reasonable officer would perceive, not the officer's personal fear alone.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a training continuum as a mandatory ladder; the legal standard is reasonableness given the threat, not sequential steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Hindsight review is the wrong lens; reasonableness is judged by the facts known to the officer at the moment force was used.

options.a: Property theft is suspected without threat to life
options.b: Trespasser refuses to leave after verbal warning
options.c: Imminent threat of death or serious bodily harm to self or others
options.d: A suspect flees from a completed felony with no continuing threat to anyone

distractorExplanations.d: Applies an old fleeing-felon idea to private officers; flight without an ongoing deadly threat does not justify deadly force.
distractorExplanations.a: Property crimes alone usually do not justify deadly force.
distractorExplanations.b: Simple trespass may not justify deadly force.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-l.explanation: Deadly force is reserved for imminent deadly threats; property alone rarely justifies it. A fleeing person or property loss, without a deadly threat, does not by itself meet that threshold. Exact deadly-force rules are set by state law.

options.a: Arrest the person for felony trespass and transport them to the police station in a patrol car
options.b: Issue a written trespass warning but take no further action until the person returns a second time
options.c: Detain the person on site until they sign a no-trespass agreement, then release them without notifying the police
options.d: Request departure, document, and contact law enforcement; use reasonable force if subject resists lawful removal

distractorExplanations.a: Posted-property trespass is usually a misdemeanor, and private officers hand the subject to police rather than transporting them.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses giving notice with enforcement; once warned, a person who stays can be asked to leave and police contacted right away.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding someone to coerce a signature exceeds lawful detention; any detention must be reasonable and end with police contact.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-l.explanation: Trespass enforcement follows warn, escort, and law enforcement coordination with reasonable force if necessary. Any force must stay within employer policy.

options.a: Government action triggers protection; private employer searches follow policy/consent
options.b: Private guards must obtain a warrant or probable cause before any workplace bag search
options.c: Protection applies only when the employer is a publicly traded company with federal contracts
options.d: Private guards are bound like police once they hold a state-issued armed security license

distractorExplanations.b: Applies warrant and probable-cause rules meant for state actors to private guards; private searches rest on policy and consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses corporate status with state action; a public company is still a private actor unless it acts for the government.
distractorExplanations.d: A state license alone does not make a guard a state actor; state action requires government direction or delegated police power.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-l.explanation: Constitutional search limits primarily bind state actors; private searches governed by policy, contract, and state tort law. Constitutional claims against purely private searches are limited.

options.a: Probable cause plus a signed complaint from the store manager before any stop
options.b: Reasonable cause, reasonable time/method, and for investigation on premises
options.c: Suspicion arises anywhere in the mall, allowing pursuit and detention off premises
options.d: Reasonable cause, with detention lasting until the suspect confesses or pays

distractorExplanations.a: Sets the bar at probable cause and a written complaint; the privilege needs reasonable cause plus reasonable time and manner.
distractorExplanations.c: The privilege is generally limited to the premises or immediate vicinity; it is not a roving authority across the whole mall.
distractorExplanations.d: Right standard but wrong purpose and duration; holding someone to extract a confession or payment makes the detention unreasonable.

options.a: Handcuff and search the person for evidence of the offense, then call police once a statement is written
options.b: Question the person until a written statement is signed, then notify police and release the subject to them
options.c: State the reason when safe, use only reasonable restraint, monitor the person, and transfer promptly to law enforcement
options.d: Release the person once identification is copied and photographed, since police transfer is required only for felony offenses

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a weapons safety check with an evidence search; private officers generally lack authority to search a detainee for evidence.
distractorExplanations.b: Prolonging the detention to obtain a statement makes it unreasonable in duration; police should be notified promptly.
distractorExplanations.d: Misreads the duty; a lawful detention ends with prompt transfer to police, not an ID copy and release based on offense grade.

options.a: Apply one level of force above the subject's resistance so the officer stays in firm control
options.b: Match the response to the behavior and threat, de-escalating or disengaging when feasible
options.c: Move through a fixed sequence of force levels even when the threat changes
options.d: Continue force after the person is controlled to ensure compliance

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a 'one-plus' escalation rule rather than proportionality; force must match the threat, not deliberately exceed it.
distractorExplanations.c: Force is not a mandatory step-by-step ladder; the response must track the actual threat and available options.
distractorExplanations.d: Force that was initially justified may become excessive once resistance or danger ends.

options.a: Subject is in custodial interrogation by law enforcement
options.b: Private security asks routine ID questions on private property
options.c: A suspect is arrested, even if police ask no questions about the offense
options.d: Police ask on-scene questions before the person is detained or arrested

distractorExplanations.c: Custody alone does not trigger Miranda; the warnings are needed when custody and police interrogation occur together.
distractorExplanations.d: General on-scene questioning of a person who is free to leave is not custodial; Miranda attaches with custody plus interrogation.
distractorExplanations.b: Private security is not Miranda agent generally.

options.a: Facts learned later in the investigation, viewed with hindsight
options.b: Totality of circumstances at time force was used
options.c: Whether a less-intrusive option was available at that moment
options.d: The subject's criminal record discovered after the incident

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 20/20 hindsight; Graham v. Connor judges force by the facts known to the officer at the moment it was used.
distractorExplanations.c: Courts do not require the least intrusive option; force only needs to be reasonable under the totality of circumstances.
distractorExplanations.d: A record discovered later was unknown at the moment of force and cannot justify it; only facts then known to the officer count.

options.a: No action, because a carry permit overrides a property owner's posted firearm ban
options.b: Detain the person at gunpoint until police arrive, treating the firearm-policy breach as a felony
options.c: Policy-based enforcement, request to leave/store weapon, and law enforcement if noncompliant
options.d: Take the firearm into custody and return it when the visitor leaves the property

distractorExplanations.a: In most states a carry permit does not override a private owner's right to exclude firearms from the property.
distractorExplanations.b: A firearm-policy violation is usually trespass at most; holding someone at gunpoint without a deadly threat is excessive force.
distractorExplanations.d: Seizing a lawfully owned firearm requires legal authority; the officer asks the person to store it off site or leave.

options.a: Review the order and site plan, enforce listed access restrictions, and coordinate with supervisors and police
options.b: Assume the order authorizes the officer to arrest the restrained person anywhere
options.c: Wait until police serve a copy of the order on the security company before acting on its access terms
options.d: Treat the order as binding the protected employee too, and remove her from the site if she contacts the restrained person

distractorExplanations.c: The site can act on its own access rules once it knows of the order; security does not need formal service before acting.
distractorExplanations.d: A protective order restrains the respondent, not the protected person; she cannot violate it by making contact.
distractorExplanations.b: A court order does not automatically give a private officer statewide police powers.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-l.explanation: The officer should know the order’s actual terms and follow the site response plan. Access control, timely notification, careful documentation, and police coordination are safer than improvising authority. Document every contact with the restrained person.

options.a: Following policy is relevant, but the officer can still face liability for unlawful or unreasonable conduct
options.b: Company policy overrides state criminal law whenever the officer is on duty
options.c: Liability shifts to the client site because the client wrote the post orders that the officer was following
options.d: Only the employer can be sued because the officer acted within the scope of employment

distractorExplanations.c: Post orders do not transfer liability to the client; the officer and the security employer remain accountable for the conduct.
distractorExplanations.d: Respondeat superior adds employer liability; it does not shield the officer from personal civil or criminal liability.
distractorExplanations.b: An employer’s policy cannot override criminal or licensing law.

options.a: Force used and injuries, with witness names left out to protect their privacy
options.b: Subject behavior, threat, commands given, force used, injuries, witnesses, and medical aid
options.c: The officer's conclusions that the subject was combative, without describing specific actions
options.d: Commands and force used, written after the shift once the supervisor has reviewed the video

distractorExplanations.a: Omits threat, commands and witnesses; witness identities are needed for review and are protected by policy rather than omitted.
distractorExplanations.c: Conclusory labels like 'combative' are weak; the report must describe the observable behavior that justified each force decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Reports should be prompt and independent; waiting to watch video first undermines the officer's own record of perception.

options.a: Draw and identify as security, then pursue the suspect to make a citizen's arrest
options.b: Take no action, since an off-duty officer loses the legal ability to make a citizen's arrest
options.c: Call 911, observe safely, intervene only within training/policy and law if imminent harm
options.d: Fire warning shots to stop the suspect from fleeing with the stolen property

distractorExplanations.a: Pursuit and arrest off duty escalate risk without backup; observing and calling 911 come first unless harm is imminent.
distractorExplanations.b: Citizen's arrest authority does not depend on duty status; the real limits are safety, training and policy, not lost authority.
distractorExplanations.d: Warning shots are prohibited by most policies, and property loss does not justify discharging a firearm in a public mall.

options.a: Treat every gun as loaded, keep the manual safety engaged until ready to fire, point downrange, and rely on the safety as a backup
options.b: Treat a gun as unloaded after a chamber check, keep finger off trigger, and know your target and backstop
options.c: Treat every gun as loaded, point in a safe direction, finger on trigger when drawn, know target and beyond
options.d: Treat every gun as loaded, never point at anything not intended to shoot, finger off trigger until ready, know target and beyond

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes reliance on a mechanical safety for trigger discipline; safeties can fail and are not one of the four core rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the first rule: every gun is treated as loaded even after checking, because a chamber check can be wrong or misread.
distractorExplanations.c: The finger stays off the trigger until the sights are on target and the decision to fire is made, not merely once drawn.

options.a: Follow the written unloading and storage procedure, keep the muzzle in a safe direction, and secure the firearm against unauthorized access
options.b: Unload the firearm and hang it holstered on the duty belt in the shared locker room for the next officer to take over
options.c: Store it unloaded in the locked glove box of a personal vehicle with the magazine kept separately in the trunk
options.d: Clear the chamber but leave a loaded magazine seated so the next shift is ready, then lock the firearm in the approved storage safe

distractorExplanations.b: An unlocked shared area is not secure storage; a shift handover needs controlled access and a logged transfer.
distractorExplanations.c: A glove box is not employer-approved storage, and many policies forbid keeping duty firearms in personal vehicles.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving a loaded magazine seated skips the written unloading procedure; readiness for the next shift is not a storage condition.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-w.explanation: End-of-shift handling must follow employer policy, state law, and the firearm manufacturer’s safety instructions. Controlled access and accurate transfer or storage records prevent theft and negligent handling. Complete any required storage or transfer log.

options.a: Tap the magazine and rack the slide repeatedly, the drill used for a failure to fire
options.b: Stop, point safe, identify malfunction type, and follow trained clearance procedure
options.c: Rack the slide hard several times to force the stuck rounds into the chamber
options.d: Lock the slide back, then pull the trigger to release tension before removing the magazine

distractorExplanations.a: Tap-rack clears a failure to fire; a double feed needs the slide locked back and the magazine stripped out first.
distractorExplanations.c: Racking alone cannot clear two rounds competing for the chamber; the magazine must be removed to release them.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling the trigger during clearance is unsafe and does nothing; the sequence is lock slide, strip magazine, rack.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-w.explanation: Complex malfunctions require proper clearance sequence; muzzle discipline maintained. An officer should use only the clearance method taught for the issued firearm and seek an instructor or armorer if it remains unsafe. A common double-feed clearance is to lock the slide, strip the magazine, rack several times, then reload.

options.a: Any factory load in the correct caliber, including +P+ rounds the maker does not rate
options.b: Commercially reloaded ammunition in the right caliber, chosen for lower cost
options.c: The load the officer qualified with last year, even if the employer has changed it
options.d: Manufacturer specifications for firearm and approved duty load by employer

distractorExplanations.a: Correct caliber is not enough; +P+ loads the manufacturer does not rate can overpressure and damage the firearm.
distractorExplanations.b: Reloads are generally barred for duty use because their quality and pressure are not controlled to factory duty standards.
distractorExplanations.c: Duty carry must match the currently approved load; qualifying with an older load does not authorize carrying it now.

options.a: Control the muzzle in a safe direction, keep the trigger finger indexed, and prevent the weapon from sweeping others
options.b: Carry the long gun at low ready pointed at the floor near teammates' feet when movement becomes crowded
options.c: Keep the finger resting on the trigger with the safety engaged so the weapon is ready the moment a threat appears
options.d: Let the sling hang the long gun freely behind the back so both hands stay open for the railing while climbing stairs

distractorExplanations.b: Pointing near teammates' feet still sweeps them; the muzzle must avoid every person, not just their upper body.
distractorExplanations.c: A safety does not replace trigger discipline; the finger stays indexed outside the guard until the decision to fire is made.
distractorExplanations.d: An uncontrolled slung weapon can swing, snag, or point at others; the officer keeps a hand on it to control the muzzle.

options.a: Draw the firearm immediately so the subject cannot reach it in the holster
options.b: Protect weapon from takeaway, create distance, and call for backup
options.c: Unload the firearm during the struggle so a takeaway would leave it harmless
options.d: Release the holster's retention device so a fast draw is possible if needed

distractorExplanations.a: Drawing during a close struggle exposes the gun to a grab; retention means securing the holstered weapon and creating space.
distractorExplanations.c: Unloading mid-struggle takes both hands off control and is not a trained retention technique.
distractorExplanations.d: Defeating the holster's retention makes a takeaway easier; retention devices stay engaged during a physical struggle.

options.a: Remove the magazine, disassemble per manual, clean bore and action, and reassemble without a chamber check
options.b: Unload and verify, then soak the assembled pistol in WD-40 and store it wet without inspection
options.c: Unload verify, disassemble per manual, clean bore/action, inspect, function check with dummy if policy
options.d: Unload and verify, clean only the barrel bore, and skip inspection because it was fired today

distractorExplanations.a: Skips verifying the chamber is empty; removing the magazine alone can leave a live round chambered during cleaning.
distractorExplanations.b: Penetrating oil is not a bore cleaner, and skipping inspection misses wear; follow the manufacturer's cleaning steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning the bore alone ignores the action, and recent firing is exactly when inspection should catch wear or damage.

options.a: Use the employer-approved procedure in a safe location while maintaining muzzle and trigger discipline
options.b: Rely on the loaded-chamber indicator and slide feel, skipping the visual and physical check
options.c: Remove the magazine first and treat the firearm as clear once the magazine well is empty
options.d: Point the muzzle at the floor of the occupied guard booth and dry-fire once to confirm the chamber is empty

distractorExplanations.b: A loaded-chamber indicator can fail or be misread; it supplements but does not replace the approved visual and physical check.
distractorExplanations.c: A round can remain chambered after the magazine is removed; the chamber must be checked separately before the gun is clear.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry-firing is not a condition check, and an occupied booth floor is neither a safe direction nor an approved clearing location.

options.a: Follow state law and employer policy, use an approved secured container, and control access
options.b: Place the firearm loose under the driver’s seat for quick access
options.c: Lock it in the trunk loaded and chambered, since transport rules match the on-duty carry rules
options.d: Allow an unlicensed passenger to carry it into the training site

distractorExplanations.c: Off-duty transport rules often differ from duty carry; many jurisdictions require the firearm unloaded and cased in transit.
distractorExplanations.b: A loose firearm can shift, become accessible, or be handled negligently.
distractorExplanations.d: Transfer to an unauthorized person can violate law, policy, and chain-of-custody controls.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-w.explanation: Transport rules vary by jurisdiction and employer. The officer must use the required container and loaded or unloaded condition, maintain control, and comply with any ammunition-separation or vehicle-storage rules. Avoid leaving the firearm unattended in the vehicle when possible.

options.a: Unload and secure the firearm, then report it at the end of the shift since no one was hurt
options.b: Pick up the casing and patch the damage, notify the supervisor, and complete the written report the next day
options.c: Secure scene, render aid if needed, notify supervisor/law enforcement, preserve evidence, complete report
options.d: Notify the supervisor, but skip law enforcement and a written report because no injury occurred

distractorExplanations.a: A no-injury discharge still requires immediate notification; delaying the report breaches policy and hampers the review.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the casing and repairing damage destroys evidence; the scene is preserved and documented before any cleanup.
distractorExplanations.d: Many policies and some laws require reporting every discharge even without injury; the absence of injury does not waive it.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-w.explanation: Negligent discharge requires immediate reporting, investigation, and remedial training. The officer must secure the scene, request medical help if needed, preserve evidence, and give a truthful account of the event. Notification follows the employer's policy and state reporting rules.

options.a: Target focus with the rear sight sharp and the front sight blurred
options.b: Rear sight focus with the front post set above the rear notch
options.c: Front sight focus with the post sunk to the bottom edge of the notch
options.d: Front sight focus with equal height sights aligned on target

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses iron-sight focus; the front sight should be sharp while the rear sight and target are slightly blurred.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong focal plane and wrong alignment; the front post sits level with the top of the rear sight, not above it.
distractorExplanations.c: Front sight focus is right, but the top of the post must be level with the rear notch, not sunk to its bottom edge.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-w.explanation: Fundamental marksmanship uses front sight focus and proper alignment for accuracy. Written knowledge does not replace supervised range training, and sight use must follow the issued system and instructor guidance. These are iron-sight fundamentals.

options.a: Prohibited or restricted by policy and law for duty use
options.b: Recommended by most contracts because it defeats body armor
options.c: Permitted for duty if the officer holds an armed guard license
options.d: Preferred for urban posts because it reduces ricochet risk

distractorExplanations.b: Duty loads favor controlled expansion and low overpenetration; AP rounds raise backstop risk and are often restricted.
distractorExplanations.c: An armed license authorizes carrying a firearm, not restricted ammunition; AP rules come from federal and state law and policy.
distractorExplanations.d: AP rounds overpenetrate and are not chosen to limit ricochet; expanding duty rounds are favored to reduce pass-through.

options.a: Justify pointing the firearm at anyone who is illuminated in the beam
options.b: Identify friend/foe and legal target while maintaining muzzle discipline
options.c: Replace verbal commands, since the light alone signals lawful authority to stop
options.d: Disorient a subject so force can be used before identification occurs

distractorExplanations.a: Illumination is for identification; lighting a person does not justify covering them with the muzzle.
distractorExplanations.c: A light does not substitute for verbal identification and commands, which are still given when feasible.
distractorExplanations.d: Disorientation is a side effect, not permission to use force; positive identification precedes any force decision.

options.a: Enter and clear the building alone, then report to control once the inside is checked
options.b: Close and lock the door, then continue the patrol without logging the finding
options.c: Secure area if safe, investigate with backup/light, report to control, document
options.d: Call police and leave the door untouched until morning management arrives

distractorExplanations.a: Solo clearing of a possible breach is unsafe; the officer reports to control and waits for backup before entering.
distractorExplanations.b: An open door may mean a breach already occurred; securing it without investigating or logging leaves the incident unexamined.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the door open until morning leaves the site exposed; the officer secures and investigates when it is safe.

options.a: Identical hourly routes so the client can verify each checkpoint time
options.b: Fully randomized, with critical points visited when time allows
options.c: Focused on the main entrance, with other critical areas checked once per shift
options.d: Varied and unpredictable to deter surveillance while covering critical points

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed timing lets offenders predict gaps; checkpoint records can be verified without identical schedules.
distractorExplanations.b: Unpredictability must not drop critical points; required checkpoints are covered every patrol cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Concentrating on one entrance leaves perimeter and interior gaps; patrols must keep covering every critical point.

options.a: Systematic search of protected area, verify cause, reset only after clearance, log details
options.b: Reset the alarm first, then search the protected area if the same zone activates again
options.c: Bypass the zone for the rest of the shift and log it for maintenance
options.d: Search the protected area, then reset it and close the log entry without recording a cause

distractorExplanations.b: Resetting before searching can erase zone data and leave an intruder inside; the area is cleared before reset.
distractorExplanations.c: Bypassing removes protection while the cause is unknown; a zone is bypassed after verification and per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Logging without a verified cause loses the record needed to spot repeat faults or an intruder probing the system.

options.a: Demand the phone and delete the photos, since site policy bans photography
options.b: Approach safely, identify, enforce site policy, notify supervisor/law enforcement if suspicious
options.c: Detain the person for police, since photographing infrastructure is a crime
options.d: Take no action unless the person enters the property, since photographing from outside is legal

distractorExplanations.a: Site policy does not authorize seizing a phone or deleting files; that requires legal authority the officer lacks.
distractorExplanations.c: Photography from a public place is usually lawful; it is a reportable indicator, not grounds for detention.
distractorExplanations.d: Lawful photography can still be a surveillance indicator; it should be noted and reported, not ignored.

options.a: Search the immediate area alone before notifying control, to avoid alarming shoppers elsewhere in the mall
options.b: Notify police only after the store-level search fails, usually after 30 minutes
options.c: Get description, notify control/PA if policy, search immediate area, coordinate with law enforcement
options.d: Broadcast the child's full name and description publicly over the PA and social media

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying notification wastes the critical early minutes; the description goes to control before or while searching.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no waiting period for a missing child; law enforcement is contacted promptly under the site protocol.
distractorExplanations.d: Public full-name broadcasts can help an abductor; Code Adam-style protocols share a description, not the child's identity.

options.a: Start and end mileage and fuel only, with incidents kept in a separate file
options.b: Incidents requiring police, with routine observations left out
options.c: Time and location of stops, completed at the end of the shift from memory
options.d: Time, location, observations, incidents, and maintenance issues

distractorExplanations.a: Mileage alone omits the patrol record; incidents and observations belong in the log as well as in reports.
distractorExplanations.b: Routine observations establish patterns and prove coverage; leaving them out weakens accountability.
distractorExplanations.c: Logs should be contemporaneous; entries reconstructed from memory at shift end lose accuracy and evidentiary weight.

options.a: Signed issuance, no unauthorized duplication, return at shift end, report lost keys immediately
options.b: Signed issuance, master keys lent to contractors on request, and return of the keys at shift end
options.c: Keys kept in the patrol car ignition so the next shift can find them quickly
options.d: Signed issuance, with lost keys reported at the next weekly security meeting

distractorExplanations.b: Master keys are not lent on request; contractors receive limited keys under written authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Unsecured keys defeat accountability; keys go back to a controlled box with a signed log.
distractorExplanations.d: Lost keys must be reported immediately so the rekey assessment starts before they can be misused.

options.a: Carry the package outdoors away from people, then call the bomb squad and the shift supervisor
options.b: Evacuate area, deny access, notify bomb squad/supervisor, avoid moving/touching package
options.c: Use a radio next to the package to update control while inspecting it
options.d: Ask nearby people who owns it and evacuate only if no one claims it

distractorExplanations.a: Moving a suspected device can trigger it; it is left in place while the area is evacuated and access denied.
distractorExplanations.c: Radio transmissions near a suspected device may set it off; communicate from a safe distance per the bomb-threat plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying evacuation to find an owner wastes time; isolate and evacuate first, then let specialists assess.

options.a: Constant flashlight use pointed ahead, with radio silence to stay covert
options.b: Visible presence with the patrol car's interior dome light on for visibility
options.c: 360 awareness, flashlight technique, visible presence, and radio check-ins
options.d: Forward focus on the lot exit, with radio check-ins at the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.a: Radio silence removes the safety check-in; night patrol relies on scheduled radio contact with control.
distractorExplanations.b: An interior light destroys night vision and silhouettes the officer; outward 360-degree awareness matters more.
distractorExplanations.d: End-of-shift contact is too late if the officer is hurt; check-ins happen at set intervals alongside 360-degree scanning.

options.a: Let a badge holder vouch for any guest who follows them through the door
options.b: Disable card readers at peak hours and rely on a guard's visual check
options.c: Challenge unknown persons, but allow groups to enter together on a single badge swipe
options.d: Challenge unknown persons, enforce one credential per entry, educate employees

distractorExplanations.a: Vouching by a badge holder is how tailgating happens; each person needs a credential or the visitor process.
distractorExplanations.b: Disabling readers removes per-person verification; a guard cannot reliably check every entrant at peak times.
distractorExplanations.c: Group entry on one swipe is tailgating by design; the rule is one credential per person per entry.

options.a: Limit access, note witness contacts, avoid contaminating evidence, brief arriving officers
options.b: Collect dropped items into a bag so they are safe for arriving officers
options.c: Clean up blood once photos are taken, before law enforcement arrives
options.d: Release witnesses once their names are taken so the scene stays uncrowded for arriving police

distractorExplanations.b: Gathering evidence moves and contaminates it; items stay in place and are pointed out to police.
distractorExplanations.c: Photos do not replace the scene; cleanup waits until police release it, apart from life-safety needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Witnesses should be asked to remain for police; names alone lose statements while memories are fresh.

options.a: Photograph the sleeping officer and post it in the team chat as a warning
options.b: Relieve post safely, notify supervisor, document objectively
options.c: Wake the officer, issue a warning, and say nothing if it does not recur
options.d: Notify the client directly before the security supervisor so the site is aware

distractorExplanations.a: Sharing images with peers is unprofessional and humiliating; the matter goes through the chain of command instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Sleeping on post is a serious breach that must be reported; an informal warning hides a security gap.
distractorExplanations.d: Reports go through the security chain of command first; bypassing the supervisor breaks procedure.

armed-security-officer-readiness-check-p.explanation: Sleeping on post is serious; report through chain of command with factual documentation. The reporting officer should first ensure the post is covered so the misconduct does not create a second security gap. Avoid escalating into a confrontation with the coworker.

options.a: Treat the alarm as a confirmed weapon and detain the visitor at gunpoint for police
options.b: Wave the visitor through if they explain the alarm as keys or a belt buckle
options.c: Secondary screening per policy, maintain courtesy and rights, escalate if prohibited item found
options.d: Pat down the visitor immediately, without explaining the alarm or offering a hand-wand scan first

distractorExplanations.a: A detector alarm calls for secondary screening; it does not confirm a weapon or justify holding someone at gunpoint.
distractorExplanations.b: A verbal explanation does not resolve an alarm; the item must be confirmed by secondary screening before entry.
distractorExplanations.d: Secondary screening follows the site procedure, usually a wand or bag check with consent, not an unexplained pat-down.

options.a: Daily log records specific events in detail; the incident report summarizes the routine shift
options.b: Incident reports are written only when police are called; logs cover all other events
options.c: Daily logs are informal internal notes that can be edited later; incident reports are the final records
options.d: Daily log summarizes routine patrol; incident report details specific event with witnesses/evidence

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the two documents; the log is the routine summary and the incident report holds the event detail.
distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are required for any significant event, not just those where police were called.
distractorExplanations.c: Both are business records that must be accurate and must not be altered after the fact.

options.a: Hydration, shade breaks, breathable gear, and recognizing early symptoms
options.b: Drinking water only when thirsty, to avoid overhydration on long shifts
options.c: Salt tablets with limited water to retain fluid during heavy sweating
options.d: Working through dizziness until the scheduled break, then resting in shade

distractorExplanations.b: Thirst lags behind fluid loss; scheduled hydration is recommended during heat exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Salt tablets are not recommended without medical advice; water and electrolyte drinks are preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: Dizziness is an early heat-illness sign that needs immediate cooling and notification, not delay.

options.a: A contract violation handled by the employer, not a criminal matter
options.b: Felony/unethical conduct leading to termination and prosecution
options.c: Acceptable if disclosed to a supervisor after the fact
options.d: Misconduct only if the theft exceeds the felony dollar threshold

distractorExplanations.a: Taking a bribe to ignore theft is a crime as well as a contract breach, so it can be prosecuted.
distractorExplanations.c: Disclosure after the fact does not cure a bribe accepted to look away from theft.
distractorExplanations.d: Bribery is illegal at any amount; theft value thresholds affect theft charges, not the bribe itself.

options.a: Report it only if the visitor files a formal complaint
options.b: Address it privately with the colleague later and keep the whole matter off the record
options.c: Interrupt behavior, report to supervisor/HR per policy, support professional conduct
options.d: Apologize to the visitor and wait to see if the behavior repeats

distractorExplanations.a: The duty to report observed harassment does not depend on a complaint from the person targeted.
distractorExplanations.b: Informal handling hides a policy violation; observed harassment is reported to a supervisor or HR.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for a repeat leaves misconduct unaddressed; it should be interrupted and reported now.

options.a: Accepts overtime shifts offered through the posted company overtime rotation list
options.b: Reports a coworker's policy violation to the shift supervisor
options.c: Holds a second job at a non-competing business on off-duty days
options.d: Has financial/personal interest affecting impartial performance of duties

distractorExplanations.a: Taking offered overtime under the normal rotation is routine employment, not a competing interest.
distractorExplanations.b: Reporting violations is a professional duty and shows impartiality rather than a conflict.
distractorExplanations.c: Outside work is not a conflict unless it competes with or affects duties; a non-competing disclosed job is not one.

options.a: Calm voice, active listening, increased distance, offering choices when safe
options.b: Loud, repeated commands at close range to show the officer is in control
options.c: Closing distance quickly so the subject has no time to become physically aggressive
options.d: Giving ultimatums with a single option to speed up compliance

distractorExplanations.b: Shouting at close range tends to escalate; de-escalation relies on a calm voice and space.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing distance removes reaction time and raises tension; de-escalation increases distance.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultimatums corner the subject; offering choices lets the person comply while saving face.

options.a: Refuse, preserve any relevant message, and report the request through the required channel
options.b: Enter the hours because coworkers are expected to protect one another
options.c: Refuse, but take no further action since a single request is not misconduct
options.d: Confront the coworker publicly at shift change so the rest of the team knows the request was made

distractorExplanations.c: Soliciting a false business record is itself misconduct that policy requires to be reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Public confrontation is unprofessional and can taint any inquiry; the request is reported through the proper channel.
distractorExplanations.b: Loyalty to a coworker does not justify a false business record.

options.a: Policy allowing personal posts while on duty as long as the client's name, logo and address are not shown
options.b: Policy allowing photos of the post if they are shared in a private group only
options.c: Policy prohibiting disclosure of post details, filming security vulnerabilities, or unprofessional posts
options.d: Personal judgment, since posts about work are protected free speech

distractorExplanations.a: Hiding the client name does not protect post details or vulnerabilities visible in on-duty photos and posts.
distractorExplanations.b: Private groups still leak; images can expose cameras, codes, and schedules to outsiders.
distractorExplanations.d: The First Amendment limits government, not private employers; confidentiality policy still applies to the officer.

options.a: Acceptable if the relationship began before the investigation
options.b: A private matter unless the officer receives money or gifts
options.c: Permitted if the officer reports the person's activities to supervisors
options.d: Conflict of interest requiring disclosure and reassignment

distractorExplanations.a: Timing does not cure it; any personal relationship with a subject under investigation must be disclosed.
distractorExplanations.b: Conflicts are not limited to financial benefit; personal relationships can also compromise impartiality.
distractorExplanations.c: Using a romantic relationship as an informant channel compounds the conflict rather than curing it.

options.a: Encourage reporting illegal/unethical conduct in good faith with anti-retaliation provisions
options.b: Protect good-faith reports only if they are first made to outside media
options.c: Protect managers and supervisors, with line officers covered by the union's grievance process instead
options.d: Protect any report, including allegations the reporter knows to be false

distractorExplanations.b: Protection generally depends on authorized internal or regulatory channels, not on going to the media first.
distractorExplanations.c: Whistleblower policies cover all employees; they are not limited to managers and supervisors.
distractorExplanations.d: Knowingly false reports are not protected; good faith is the condition for anti-retaliation coverage.

options.a: Report the incident at the end of shift after discussing it with the partner
options.b: Intervene if safe, report immediately, document facts objectively
options.c: Document the facts but report only if the subject files a complaint
options.d: Intervene physically in every case, even when it endangers bystanders

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting must be immediate and independent; discussing it with the partner first risks a coordinated account.
distractorExplanations.c: The duty to report observed excessive force does not wait for a complaint from the subject.
distractorExplanations.d: Intervention is required when safe; it does not demand action that puts bystanders at greater risk.

options.a: Accepted if the officer reports it on the next annual form
options.b: Accepted because gifts after a service are not bribes
options.c: Declined or disclosed per anti-gratuity policy
options.d: Shared with the whole shift so no single officer benefits

distractorExplanations.a: Late annual disclosure does not address a $200 gift timed with contract renewal; policy requires decline or prompt disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Timing during renewal creates an appearance of influence whether or not an explicit quid pro quo exists.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing does not remove the gratuity concern; the gift still comes from a protected party during renewal.

options.a: Adjusting enforcement for each culture's norms so no group feels singled out
options.b: Treating everyone identically by ignoring language or disability needs
options.c: Avoiding contact with groups the officer is unfamiliar with in order to prevent any offense
options.d: Respecting diverse backgrounds while enforcing rules consistently and professionally

distractorExplanations.a: Varying rule enforcement by culture is unequal treatment; rules apply consistently based on conduct.
distractorExplanations.b: Consistent enforcement still allows reasonable language access and accessibility accommodations.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoidance leads to uneven protection; competency means professional engagement with everyone.

options.a: Use EAP/critical incident debrief resources per policy
options.b: Return to full duty the next shift to process it through routine
options.c: Seek support only if symptoms persist beyond six months
options.d: Discuss the shooting details with coworkers before giving a statement

distractorExplanations.b: Immediate return without support or evaluation can worsen trauma; many policies include administrative leave.
distractorExplanations.c: Early support after a critical incident is encouraged; waiting months lets trauma symptoms entrench.
distractorExplanations.d: Discussing facts before statements can contaminate the investigation; use confidential support channels.

options.a: Comply, since the supervisor bears the responsibility for the order
options.b: Refuse falsification and report if necessary through ethics channel
options.c: Backdate the entry but add a note that it was done at the supervisor's request
options.d: Refuse, and then delete the original entry to avoid any dispute later

distractorExplanations.a: Following an order to falsify records does not shield the officer; both can be held responsible.
distractorExplanations.c: A noted backdate is still a falsified record; the original entry must stay intact.
distractorExplanations.d: Deleting the original entry destroys a business record and is itself misconduct.

options.a: Giving VIPs discretion on minor rules whenever the client informally asks the officer for it
options.b: Focusing enforcement on groups with the most past incidents
options.c: Applying site rules equally regardless of status, unless policy provides lawful exception
options.d: Applying rules strictly to visitors but giving employees informal warnings for the same conduct

distractorExplanations.a: Informal client requests are not lawful written exceptions; unequal enforcement erodes trust.
distractorExplanations.b: Group-based targeting is profiling; enforcement must be based on individual behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Different treatment by status is selective enforcement unless written policy lawfully provides for it.

options.a: Follow the code as written when signed, with later updates optional until re-signing
options.b: Follow the code while on duty, with off-duty conduct outside the employer's concern
options.c: Report violations to coworkers first so they can correct them before supervisors find out
options.d: Follow policies on honesty, confidentiality, force, appearance, and reporting violations

distractorExplanations.a: Acknowledgment covers ongoing compliance, including updates issued after the original signature.
distractorExplanations.b: Codes often reach off-duty conduct that affects licensing, integrity, or the client relationship.
distractorExplanations.c: Violations are reported through the designated channel, not resolved informally among peers.
